# Mia: full guides

> Pregnancy, birth and after-birth guides from Mia (https://miapregnancy.com). Education, not medical advice. Always contact a midwife or doctor for concerns.

# Pregnancy week by week: what to expect from week 1 to 40
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pregnancy-week-by-week/
Stage: Pregnancy

Each week of pregnancy brings small changes for you and your baby. Mia shows your week at a glance: how big your baby is, what your body is doing and one thing worth doing now.

## In short
- Weeks 1 to 12: The first trimester. Tiredness and nausea are common. Your dating scan is offered at 11 to 14 weeks.
- Weeks 13 to 27: The second trimester. Many people feel more energy. You may feel the first movements.
- Weeks 28 to 40: The third trimester. Get to know your baby’s usual pattern of movements and call if it changes.
- After 40 weeks: Many babies arrive after their due date. Your midwife will talk with you about your options.

## How pregnancy is dated
Pregnancy is dated from the first day of your last period.
You are in your first trimester up to week 12, your second from week 13, and your third from week 28.

## The first trimester
In week 4 your baby is about the size of a poppy seed. By week 12 they are about the size of a plum, and many people start to feel better as the first trimester ends.
Early on you may have no symptoms at all. Common ones are a missed period, nausea, tiredness, sore breasts and needing to pee more often.

## The second trimester
By week 20 you are halfway. You may have your anomaly scan around now, and your hands, feet and gums may swell a little.
You are offered the whooping cough vaccine, usually around week 20 but any time from week 16 to 32. The protection passes to your baby through the placenta.

## The third trimester
From week 28 you will probably feel more tired and uncomfortable. Heartburn, backache and swollen ankles are common.
The RSV vaccine is recommended from around week 28. It can lower your baby’s risk of severe bronchiolitis in their first 6 months.
By week 40 you may get a lot of practice contractions. When contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every 5 minutes, call your hospital or midwife.

## Your check-ups
If this is your first baby you will be offered at least 10 antenatal appointments and 2 scans. If you have had a baby before, at least 7.
Your first midwife appointment is usually at 8 to 12 weeks. At each visit your midwife checks your blood pressure and urine, and later measures your bump and talks about your baby’s movements.
You can contact maternity services at any time if you are worried. You do not have to wait for your next appointment.

## When to call your midwife
- You are worried about your health or your baby’s
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Swelling of your face, hands or feet that comes on quickly. It may be pre-eclampsia
- Contractions lasting 60 seconds and coming every 5 minutes

## Questions
Q: How many weeks is a full pregnancy?
A: Most pregnancies are counted as around 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. Your midwife will talk through your due date and your options if you go past it.
Q: Do I have to wait for my next appointment if I am worried?
A: No. You can contact maternity services at any time, day or night.

Evidence: Based on NHS pregnancy guidance and WHO antenatal care recommendations.
Sources: Week 4 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/1st-trimester/week-4/); Week-by-week guide to pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/); Week 20 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/2nd-trimester/week-20/); Week 28 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-28/); Week 40 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-40/); Antenatal care and appointments (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/your-antenatal-care-and-appointments/)

# The first trimester: weeks 1 to 13
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/first-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

The first trimester can feel huge to you while nobody else can see anything. This guide covers what is common, what helps and when to call someone.

## In short
- Common symptoms: Tiredness, nausea, tender breasts and needing to pee more are very common.
- Nausea: Small, regular snacks and sips of water can help. If you cannot keep anything down, call your midwife or doctor.
- Your first scan: The dating scan is offered between 11 and 14 weeks.
- Call if: You have vaginal bleeding, cannot keep fluids down for 24 hours, or feel very unwell.

## What is happening
In week 4 your baby is about 2 mm long, protected by a sac of fluid. By week 8 they are about the size of a raspberry, and by week 12 about the size of a plum.
Around week 12 the placenta takes over feeding your baby from the yolk sac, and hormones often settle a little.

## How you may feel
You may have no symptoms at first. Others are a missed period, a metallic taste, sore breasts, tiredness, new likes and dislikes for food, a stronger sense of smell and needing to pee more.
Light spotting can happen, but see a doctor if you have bleeding in pregnancy.
If this is your first pregnancy you might not start showing until at least week 12.

## Morning sickness
Nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy is very common. It can happen at any time of day and usually clears up by weeks 16 to 20. It does not put your baby at increased risk.
Things to try: rest, dry toast or a plain biscuit in the morning, small frequent meals of plain foods, cold foods if smells bother you, and sipping fluids. Ginger and acupressure bands may help.
A severe form is called hyperemesis gravidarum. Call your midwife, GP or 111 if you cannot keep food or fluids down for 24 hours, have very dark urine or have not peed in 8 hours, feel faint, have tummy pain or a high temperature, or vomit blood.

## Looking after yourself
You may feel anxious or stressed at times. Rest as much as you can, eat small healthy meals, and share your worries with your midwife or doctor.
Try to follow a healthy diet. You do not need to eat more for the baby in the first trimester.

## Your first appointment
Refer yourself to NHS maternity services as soon as you know you are pregnant. Your first midwife appointment is usually at 8 to 12 weeks and can take about an hour.
Your midwife asks about your health, checks your blood pressure and urine, offers a blood test for your blood group, and gives you your maternity notes.
Between 11 and 14 weeks you are offered a dating scan. It checks when your baby is due and whether you are having more than one baby. Screening tests at this scan are your choice.

## When to call your midwife
- Bleeding from your vagina
- You cannot keep food or fluids down for 24 hours
- Very dark urine, or no pee for more than 8 hours
- Tummy pain, a high temperature, or you vomit blood
- You feel very weak, dizzy or faint

## Questions
Q: When should I see a midwife?
A: As soon as you know you are pregnant, refer yourself to NHS maternity services. Your first midwife appointment is usually at 8 to 12 weeks.
Q: Is morning sickness harmful to my baby?
A: No. It is unpleasant, but it does not put your baby at increased risk. Call your midwife or GP if you cannot keep fluids down.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on the first trimester and NICE antenatal care guidance.
Sources: Week 4 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/1st-trimester/week-4/); Week 8 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/1st-trimester/week-8/); Week 12 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/1st-trimester/week-12/); Vomiting and morning sickness (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/common-symptoms/vomiting-and-morning-sickness/); Antenatal care and appointments (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/your-antenatal-care-and-appointments/)

# The second trimester: weeks 14 to 27
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/second-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

Many people feel their best in the second trimester. This guide covers the changes, the scan and what to watch for.

## In short
- More energy: Nausea often eases and energy returns for many people.
- The anomaly scan: Usually offered at 18 to 21 weeks. It checks how baby is growing.
- First movements: You may feel flutters from around 16 to 24 weeks.
- Common aches: Back, hip and round ligament pain are common. Gentle movement and rest can help.

## Halfway
Week 20 is the halfway point. By week 27 you are two-thirds of the way through.
Many people are past the worst of their early symptoms by now.

## What you may notice
Common signs are tiredness, stretch marks, swollen or bleeding gums, round ligament pains on the sides of your belly, nosebleeds, leg cramps, bloating and heartburn.
Sudden sharp calf pains at night are probably cramp. Rub the muscle hard or pull your toes up towards your ankle.
Bloating and constipation are partly your growing baby and partly the hormone progesterone. Drink water, choose high-fibre foods and eat plenty of fruit and vegetables.

## Your baby’s movements
Most people feel their baby move between 16 and 24 weeks. If this is your first baby you might not feel movements until after 20 weeks. Tell your midwife if you have not felt movement by 24 weeks.

## Your 20-week scan
The 20-week scan, also called the anomaly scan, is usually done between 18 and 21 weeks. It checks your baby’s growth and looks for 11 different conditions.
The scan may not find everything. It also checks your placenta and the blood flow in your womb. It is always offered.

## Vaccines and paperwork
The whooping cough vaccine is usually offered around week 20, but you can have it any time from week 16 to week 32.
From week 20 you can ask your doctor or midwife for a maternity certificate (MAT B1). You need it to claim maternity pay and benefits.

## Sleep and travel
The NHS advises sleeping on either side rather than on your back. After week 28, research suggests sleeping on your back can double the risk of stillbirth. Support your bump with a pillow and put another between your knees.
Do not worry if you roll onto your back in the night. Just roll onto your side again.
Around week 27 is probably the last week you can fly without a fitness to fly note. After that you need a note from your midwife or doctor. Check your airline’s cut-off dates.

## Your appointments
You are offered a 16-week appointment, the 18 to 21 week scan and, if this is your first baby, a 25-week appointment. At these visits your midwife checks your blood pressure and urine and, from 25 weeks, measures your bump.
If you have a higher chance of gestational diabetes you are offered testing between 24 and 28 weeks.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby moves less than usual, or you have not felt movement by 24 weeks
- Bleeding from your vagina
- You are worried about anything. You do not have to wait for your next appointment

## Questions
Q: When will I feel my baby move?
A: Between 16 and 24 weeks. If this is your first baby you might not feel movements until after 20 weeks. Tell your midwife if you have not felt movement by 24 weeks.
Q: Which side is best to sleep on?
A: Either side is better than your back. Use pillows to support your bump and keep your knees bent.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on the second trimester and the NHS fetal anomaly screening programme.
Sources: Week 20 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/2nd-trimester/week-20/); Week 27 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/2nd-trimester/week-27/); Week-by-week guide to pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/); The 20-week screening scan (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/20-week-scan/); Antenatal care and appointments (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/your-antenatal-care-and-appointments/); Your baby’s movements (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/your-babys-movements/)

# The third trimester: weeks 28 to 40
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/third-trimester/
Stage: Pregnancy

The last stretch brings big changes. This guide helps you get ready and know when to call.

## In short
- Baby grows fast: Baby puts on weight and gets into position for birth, often head down.
- Know the movements: Learn your baby’s usual pattern and call the same day if it changes.
- Get ready: Finish your birth plan, pack your bag and plan the journey to your birth place.
- Call if: You have bleeding, your baby moves less, or you have sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet.

## What to expect
From week 28 you will probably feel more uncomfortable and tired. Heartburn, indigestion and backache are common, and your joints and ligaments are looser than usual.
Ankles, feet and face can puff up, especially when it is hot. This is probably water retention, but get it checked in case it is pre-eclampsia, where you can feel well while your blood pressure rises dangerously high very quickly.
If you are worried about anything, talk to your midwife or doctor, or call NHS 111.

## Vaccines
The RSV vaccine is recommended at around week 28, and can be given later, right up until labour. It can lower the risk of severe bronchiolitis in your baby’s first 6 months by about 70%.
If you have not had the whooping cough vaccine, you can have it up to week 32. Speak to your midwife or GP.

## Your baby’s movements
Keep getting to know your baby’s usual pattern of movements. Call your midwife or maternity unit straight away if they move less than usual or the pattern changes.
Do not wait until the next day, even in the middle of the night.

## Sleep
Sleep on either side rather than on your back. After week 28, sleeping on your back may double the risk of stillbirth.

## Check-ups
At 36 weeks your midwife checks your blood pressure, urine and bump, and feels the position of your baby. These appointments can pick up changes you may not notice, such as very high blood pressure.
If your baby is not head down by 36 weeks you may be offered a turn, called ECV. It works about half the time.
At 38 and 40 weeks your midwife talks about your choices if you are still pregnant after 40 weeks.

## Planning the birth
In England about 6 in 10 births are vaginal births without help, nearly 3 in 10 are caesarean births and just over 1 in 10 are assisted with ventouse or forceps.
If you have had a caesarean before, a vaginal birth is often still possible. It depends on why you needed one. Talk it through with your midwife or doctor.
Around week 40, when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every 5 minutes, call your hospital or midwife.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Swelling of your face, hands or feet that comes on quickly
- Contractions lasting at least 60 seconds, every 5 minutes
- Your waters break, or you have vaginal bleeding
- You are worried about anything

## Questions
Q: Is it normal to feel more tired again?
A: Yes. The third trimester often brings heartburn, backache and tiredness. Rest when you can, and call your midwife if you are worried about anything.
Q: Can I bring on labour at home?
A: There are no proven ways to safely bring on labour at home. Ask your doctor or midwife before trying anything other than watching and waiting.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE antenatal care guidance.
Sources: Week 28 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-28/); Your baby’s movements (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/your-babys-movements/); Week 27 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/2nd-trimester/week-27/); Week 36 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-36/); Antenatal care and appointments (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/your-antenatal-care-and-appointments/); Week 40 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-40/)

# Baby movements: what is normal and when to call
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/baby-movements/
Stage: Pregnancy

Your baby’s movements are a sign they are doing well. Learn their usual pattern, and call if it changes.

## In short
- When you feel them: Many people feel the first movements between weeks 16 and 24. It may be later in a first pregnancy.
- Know your baby’s pattern: There is no set number of kicks. Get to know what is usual for your baby.
- Less movement: If your baby moves less than usual, call your midwife or maternity unit straight away. Do not wait until the next day.
- No home dopplers: Do not use a home doppler to check on your baby. Hearing a heartbeat does not mean your baby is well. Call your midwife.

## Why movements matter
If your baby is not well, they may be less active than usual. Less movement can be a sign of a problem, and the sooner it is found the better.
Feeling your baby move is a reassurance that they are well. A reduction or a change in the pattern is what matters.

## When you will feel them
Most people feel their baby move between 16 and 24 weeks. If this is your first baby, you might not feel movements until after 20 weeks.
Movements can feel like a gentle swirling or fluttering, then kicks, swishes, rolls and jerks as your baby grows.
If you have not felt your baby move by 24 weeks, tell your midwife. They will check your baby’s heartbeat and movements.

## What is normal
There is no set number of movements. Every baby is different, and you do not need to count kicks. What matters is getting to know your own baby’s usual pattern from day to day.
Afternoon and evening are often the busiest times. Your baby also has sleep periods, mostly 20 to 40 minutes and rarely longer than 90 minutes, when they usually do not move.
The number of movements tends to go up until about 32 weeks, then stays about the same. You should feel your baby move right up to and during labour.

## Why you may notice less
You are less likely to notice movements when you are busy or active. A placenta at the front of your womb can also make movements harder to feel.
Strong pain relief or sedatives, alcohol and smoking can make a baby move less. Sometimes a baby moves less because they are unwell.

## If movements change
Call your midwife or maternity unit straight away if your baby is moving less than usual, you cannot feel them any more, or the pattern changes. Do not wait until the next day, even in the middle of the night.
Never go to sleep ignoring a change in your baby’s movements. Call each time it happens, even if everything was fine before.
Do not use a home doppler or heartbeat kit. It is not a reliable way to check on your baby, and hearing a heartbeat does not mean your baby is well.
There is not enough evidence to recommend a movement chart as routine. Knowing your baby’s own pattern matters more.

## What care to expect
After 28 weeks you must contact your midwife or maternity unit immediately. You will be asked about the movements and checked, and your baby’s heartbeat will be listened to.
Between 24 and 28 weeks, call your midwife or unit. They will check your baby’s heartbeat and give you a full check-up. A scan may be arranged.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby is moving less than usual
- The pattern of movements changes
- You cannot feel your baby move any more. Call straight away
- You have not felt your baby move by week 24

## Questions
Q: Do I need to count kicks?
A: No. There is no set number. Get to know your baby’s usual pattern and call if it changes or slows down.
Q: Do babies move less near the end of pregnancy?
A: No. The number of movements tends to stay about the same after 32 weeks, and you should feel your baby right up to and during labour.
Q: What if I called before and everything was fine?
A: Call again each time. Midwives would rather check than have you wait.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on baby movements and Tommy’s and RCOG advice on reduced movements.
Sources: Your baby’s movements (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/your-babys-movements/); Your baby’s movements in pregnancy (https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/your-babys-movements-in-pregnancy/)

# What to eat in pregnancy and what to avoid
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pregnancy-nutrition/
Stage: Pregnancy

You do not need to eat for two. This guide covers what helps you and your baby, and which foods to avoid, without the stress.

## In short
- Eat a varied diet: Fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, protein and dairy or alternatives. You do not need to eat for two.
- Key supplements: In the UK, folic acid until week 12, and vitamin D from October to March, or all year if you get little sun.
- Foods to avoid: Avoid liver, raw or undercooked meat, raw fish and shellfish, and unpasteurised dairy. Limit tuna and oily fish.
- Caffeine and alcohol: Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, about two mugs of instant coffee. The safest choice with alcohol is none.

## Eating well
You do not need a special diet. Eat a variety of foods every day to get the nutrients you and your baby need.
You do not need to “eat for 2”, even with twins or triplets. You may be hungrier than usual, but a healthy breakfast can help you avoid snacking on foods high in fat and sugar.
You do not need to get the balance right at every meal, but try to get it right over a week.

## What to put on your plate
Aim for at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day. Fresh, frozen, canned, dried or juiced all count. Wash fresh produce carefully.
Starchy foods such as bread, potatoes, rice and pasta should make up just over a third of what you eat. Choose wholegrain or higher-fibre options where you can.
Eat some protein every day: beans, pulses, fish, eggs, poultry, lean meat and nuts. Cook poultry, burgers, sausages and whole cuts of meat until steaming hot with no pink.
Eat 2 portions of fish a week, 1 of them oily, such as salmon, sardines or mackerel. Dairy foods give you calcium. Choose low-fat versions, or unsweetened calcium-fortified alternatives.

## Vitamins
Take 400 micrograms of folic acid every day, ideally from 3 months before you conceive until the end of week 12. It lowers the chance of your baby having a neural tube defect such as spina bifida.
Some people need a higher 5 mg dose, which a GP can prescribe. This includes people with diabetes, a blood condition such as sickle cell, or who take medicine for epilepsy or HIV.
Take 10 micrograms of vitamin D every day from early October to late March. Some people need it all year, for example if you cover most of your skin outdoors or spend a lot of time indoors.
Your iron is checked at your first appointment and around 28 weeks. Do not take cod liver oil or supplements with vitamin A. Too much can harm your baby’s development.

## Foods to avoid
Avoid raw or undercooked meat, liver and liver products, game meats such as pheasant and venison, unpasteurised milk and dairy, and mould-ripened soft cheeses like brie and camembert unless cooked until steaming hot.
Avoid raw fish and raw shellfish, and swordfish, shark and marlin. Cold-smoked fish such as smoked salmon should be cooked until steaming hot.
Eggs with the British Lion stamp are safe raw or runny. Other hen eggs should be cooked until the white and yolk are firm.
Listeria bacteria can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or a very unwell newborn. That is why chilled ready-to-eat foods need care. Keep them cold and eat them before the use-by date.

## Drinks
Have no more than 200 mg of caffeine a day. That is about 2 mugs of instant coffee. A cup of tea has about 75 mg and a can of cola about 40 mg. Too much caffeine is linked to a higher chance of miscarriage and stillbirth.
Avoid alcohol. It can cause long-term harm to your baby and it is safest to avoid it. Limit herbal teas to 4 cups a day and avoid teas with liquorice root.
Limit tuna to 4 cans or 2 steaks a week, and oily fish to 2 portions a week. They can contain pollutants such as mercury.

## If you have already eaten something on the list
If you ate a small amount of something you should avoid and you did not get ill, it is unlikely to affect your baby. Talk to your midwife or GP if you are worried.
Get help from 111 if you feel unwell after eating or drinking something that should be avoided, have vomiting or diarrhoea for more than 48 hours, or have signs of listeriosis or toxoplasmosis.

## When to call your midwife
- You feel unwell after eating something on the avoid list. Call 111
- Vomiting or diarrhoea for more than 48 hours. Call 111
- You are very tired and may be low in iron. Ask your midwife for a blood test

## Questions
Q: Do I need to eat for two?
A: No. Even with twins or triplets you do not need to eat for two. Eat a healthy, varied diet.
Q: Which vitamins do I need?
A: Folic acid every day until week 12, and vitamin D from October to March, or all year if you get little sun. Avoid supplements with vitamin A.
Q: Can I have coffee?
A: Yes, up to 200 mg of caffeine a day. That is about 2 mugs of instant coffee. Tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate also count.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on foods to avoid and vitamins in pregnancy.
Sources: Have a healthy diet in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/have-a-healthy-diet/); Pregnancy vitamins and supplements (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/pregnancy-vitamins-and-supplements/); Foods to avoid in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/foods-to-avoid/)

# Exercise in pregnancy: what is safe
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/exercise-in-pregnancy/
Stage: Pregnancy

Moving in pregnancy is good for you and your baby. This guide covers what is safe, what to avoid and when to stop.

## In short
- Keep moving: About 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is advised if you are well. Walking and swimming are easy places to start.
- Strength and stretching: Gentle strength work, yoga and pelvic floor exercises are fine for most people. Tell the teacher you are pregnant.
- What to avoid: Avoid contact sports, activities with a risk of falling, and lying flat on your back for long periods later on.
- Stop and call if: You feel faint, overheated or in any pain. Call your midwife about bleeding or less baby movement.

## Is it safe
Exercise is safe for you and your baby in pregnancy. Start any new exercise gently. It is usually fine to keep doing what you already do.
Being active can keep you fit, prepare your body for birth, help your recovery, improve sleep, mood and mental health, and lower the risk of some conditions like gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia.

## How much
Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, the same advice as for all adults. You should be able to talk but not sing.
You do not need to do it all at once. Shorter sessions every day work too. Try to include 2 sessions a week of muscle strengthening, such as yoga, carrying shopping or strength training.
If you cannot reach 150 minutes, do what you can. Any activity is better than none.

## Getting started
If you are new to exercise, start with about 10 minutes a day and build up slowly.
It is not recommended to start a new vigorous activity such as running in pregnancy. If you have a health condition, ask your midwife what is safe for you.
Walking, swimming and yoga are good options. Swimming eases pressure on your muscles and joints.

## Staying safe
Tell your instructor you are pregnant. Drink water, keep cool, and stop if you feel uncomfortable, too hot or unwell.
Avoid sports with a risk of falling or bumping your tummy, such as hockey, rugby or mountain biking. Tommy’s also lists boxing, football, horse riding and climbing. Do not scuba dive, and do not exercise on an empty stomach.
In later pregnancy, avoid lying flat on your back for more than a few minutes. It can make you feel dizzy and is not good for your baby.

## Trimester by trimester
First trimester: if you were active before, carry on. If you are new to it, start gently. Do not exercise in very hot conditions, and drink plenty of fluids. Start your pelvic floor exercises.
Second trimester: think about swapping high-impact exercise like running and aerobics for walking or swimming. If you ran regularly it is fine to carry on for as long as you feel comfortable. Do not lie on your back for longer than a few minutes.
Third trimester: you can stay active right up to the birth if you feel well. Keep to low-impact activities such as walking, swimming and dancing, and slow down as your due date gets closer.

## Worries
There is no evidence that physical activity or exercise causes miscarriage or premature birth. Your baby is well protected and cushioned inside the womb. If you are at risk of complications such as premature labour, take extra care and ask your midwife.
The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. Stop straight away if you feel faint, overheated or in any pain.

## Listen to your body
As your bump grows you may find other activities more comfortable. If you used to run, brisk walking may feel better.
Do not push yourself too hard. If something does not feel right, stop and talk to your midwife.

## When to call your midwife
- You feel dizzy, faint or very unwell while exercising
- You have bleeding, fluid leaking or tummy pain
- Your baby moves less than usual
- You have a health condition and are not sure what is safe

## Questions
Q: How much exercise should I do?
A: Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, including muscle strengthening. Do what you can. Any activity is better than none.
Q: Can I keep running?
A: It is usually fine to keep doing activities you already do. It is not recommended to start a new vigorous activity in pregnancy.
Q: What should I avoid?
A: Contact sports and activities with a risk of falling, scuba diving, exercising on an empty stomach, and lying flat on your back for long in later pregnancy.

Evidence: Based on NHS and UK Chief Medical Officers’ guidance on exercise in pregnancy.
Sources: Exercise in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/keeping-well/exercise/); How active should I be in pregnancy? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/im-pregnant/exercise-in-pregnancy/how-active-should-i-be-pregnancy)

# Braxton Hicks or real labour? How to tell
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/braxton-hicks/
Stage: Pregnancy

Practice tightenings can feel strong and worrying. This guide helps you tell them from true labour.

## In short
- What they feel like: A tightening across your belly that comes and goes, often irregular and not painful.
- What helps: Change position, rest, have a warm bath and drink water.
- Signs of labour: Contractions that get stronger, longer and closer together, and do not ease with rest.
- Call if: You have regular contractions before week 37, bleeding, fluid leaking, or reduced baby movement.

## What Braxton Hicks are
Braxton Hicks are tightenings of your womb that come and go. They are sometimes called practice contractions or false labour. They are one of the ways your body gets ready for birth.
Unlike labour contractions, they do not open your cervix, the entrance to your womb. So even when they feel strong, they are not a sign that labour has started.
Not everyone notices them, and that is fine too. If you do, it is most often in the second or third trimester.

## What they feel like
Many people describe a tightening across the bump, a bit like mild period cramps. Your bump may feel hard for a minute or two, then soften again.
They can be uncomfortable, but they are usually not painful. They do not last long, they do not come often and they do not build up.
Near your due date they can feel stronger or come more often. That is why it can be hard to tell them apart from the start of labour.

## What sets them off
Nobody knows exactly why they happen. Being very active, a full bladder, sex and not drinking enough can all bring them on.
Experts think they help tone the muscles of your womb, ready for labour.

## What helps
Change what you are doing. If you have been on your feet a lot, lie down. If you have been sitting for a long time, go for a gentle walk.
A warm bath, a nap, slow breathing and a glass of water can all help them settle.

## How real labour is different
Labour contractions come at regular times and get longer, stronger and closer together. They do not ease when you rest or change position.
Labour often starts slowly. This early part, called the latent phase, can take hours or even days, and you will usually be advised to stay at home for it.
Other signs that labour may be starting are a show (a plug of pink, sticky mucus coming away), backache, needing the toilet a lot, and your waters breaking.
Your midwife will usually suggest you call when contractions come about every 5 minutes or more often.

## If labour does start
At the start of labour your cervix softens and opens. This latent phase is usually the longest part and can take many hours, sometimes days.
During the day, stay upright and gently active. At night, rest and sleep if you can. Eat and drink, because you will need energy later.
Breathing, a back rub, a warm bath or shower and paracetamol (taken as the packet says) can ease early contractions.

## Before 37 weeks
Labour before 37 weeks is called premature labour. About 8 in 100 babies are born early.
If you are less than 37 weeks and have regular tightenings, period-type pains, unusual backache or a trickle of fluid, call your maternity unit. They can check whether labour is starting.

## When tummy pain is something else
Mild pain that goes away when you rest, change position or go to the toilet is usually nothing to worry about.
Pain that is strong, or does not go away after 30 to 60 minutes of rest, needs a call to your maternity unit straight away. The same goes for pain with bleeding, fluid leaking or pain when you pee.

## When to call your midwife
- You are not sure if it is Braxton Hicks or labour
- Regular tightenings before 37 weeks
- Bleeding from your vagina, or your waters break
- Contractions lasting longer than 2 minutes, or 6 or more in 10 minutes
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Strong tummy pain that does not ease after resting

## Questions
Q: How many Braxton Hicks a day is normal?
A: There is no set number. What matters is the pattern: they stay irregular and short and ease with rest. If they become regular, call your maternity unit. If you are under 37 weeks, call if they keep going.
Q: Can Braxton Hicks hurt my baby?
A: No. They are a normal part of pregnancy. Keep noticing your baby’s usual movements, and call if they slow down or change.
Q: I am not sure what I am feeling. Is it OK to call?
A: Yes. Midwives would rather check and reassure you than have you worry at home. Maternity units are open day and night.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on Braxton Hicks and signs of labour.
Sources: Signs that labour has begun (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/signs-that-labour-has-begun/); Braxton Hicks (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/braxton-hicks); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/); Premature labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/premature-labour-and-birth/); Stomach pain in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/common-symptoms/stomach-pain/)

# Natural birth: what helps and what the evidence says
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/natural-birth/
Stage: Birth

A natural birth starts and carries on by itself, with only the medical help you need. This guide covers what tends to help, how strong the evidence is and what your other options look like.

## In short
- Move and stay upright: Walking, swaying and kneeling in early labour can help labour move along. Research links upright positions with a shorter first stage.
- Continuous support: Having one person with you the whole time, like a doula or partner, is linked with fewer interventions and a better experience.
- Eat, drink and rest: In early labour, eat and drink, rest at night if you can, and stay gently active by day.
- Every option is fine: Pain relief, induction or a caesarean can be the right choice. Mia explains them too, without judgement.

## What natural birth means
Most births in England, around 6 in 10, are vaginal births without help.
There are 3 stages of labour. In the first, contractions open your cervix to about 10 cm. In the second, your baby is born. In the third, the placenta comes out.

## The first stage
The early, or latent, phase can take many hours or even days. Eat and drink, rest at night if you can, and stay upright and gently active in the day.
Established labour starts when your cervix is about 4 cm open and contractions are stronger and more regular. In a first pregnancy the time to full dilation is usually 8 to 18 hours. It is often quicker, around 5 to 12 hours, in a second or third pregnancy.

## The second stage
Your midwife helps you find a position to give birth in. You may feel an urge to push that feels like needing to poo.
Pushing should last no longer than 3 hours with a first baby, or 2 hours if you have had one before.
The third stage, when the placenta comes out, is usually over within 30 minutes. You are offered an injection of oxytocin to help.

## Staying upright and moving
Moving around, staying upright and changing position can mean a shorter labour, less pain, fewer interventions and more sense of control.
Birth balls, kneeling, leaning on your partner and a warm bath or shower are all worth trying.

## Coping with pain
Learn about labour, practise breathing and relaxation, keep moving, and bring a support person. Paracetamol and a warm bath can help early on.
Breathing, visualisation and relaxation, as used in hypnobirthing, may help you feel more relaxed and in control.
Keep an open mind. You may want more pain relief than you planned, and that is fine. Gas and air, injections, an epidural and a birth pool are all options depending on where you give birth.

## Support
People who have continuous support in labour are less likely to have an assisted birth, a caesarean, pain relief or a longer labour.
Choose a birth partner you trust, and talk through your birth plan and wishes beforehand.

## When to call your midwife
- Contractions every 5 minutes or more often
- Your waters break, or you have vaginal bleeding
- Your baby moves less than usual
- You are under 37 weeks and think you are in labour

## Questions
Q: How long is labour?
A: In a first pregnancy, established labour to full dilation usually takes 8 to 18 hours, and often 5 to 12 in a later pregnancy. The early phase can take much longer.
Q: Do I have to avoid pain relief for a natural birth?
A: No. Keep an open mind. You can use pain relief and still have a vaginal birth.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane reviews of upright positions in labour and of continuous support in labour.
Sources: Week 36 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-36/); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/); Week 40 (https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/pregnancy/week-by-week-guide-to-pregnancy/3rd-trimester/week-40/); What happens straight after the birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/what-happens-straight-after/); Movement and positions during labour (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/movement-and-positions-during-labour); Pain relief in labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/pain-relief-in-labour/); What is hypnobirthing? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/pain-relief/hypnobirthing); What is a doula? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/labour-and-birth-faqs/what-doula)

# Signs of labour and when to call your midwife
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/signs-of-labour/
Stage: Birth

Labour often starts slowly. This guide covers the early signs, what real contractions feel like and when to call your midwife, so you are not left guessing.

## In short
- Early signs: Regular tightenings, a show (a pink or bloody mucus plug), backache or a watery trickle can all be early signs.
- Real or practice?: Practice contractions (Braxton Hicks) are irregular and ease with rest. Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together.
- When to call: Call your midwife or maternity unit if your waters break, if you bleed, if baby moves less, or if contractions are regular and strong.
- At home first: Many people stay at home in early labour: eat lightly, drink, rest and move. Your midwife will guide you on when to come in.

## The signs
Labour may be starting if you have contractions or tightenings, a “show”, backache, an urge to go to the toilet, or your waters break.
An urge to go to the toilet comes from your baby’s head pressing on your bowel.

## Contractions
In a contraction your womb tightens, then relaxes. For some people it feels like extreme period pain. Put your hand on your bump and you will feel it get hard, then ease.
Labour contractions get longer, stronger and more frequent as labour goes on. Practice contractions (Braxton Hicks) are usually painless, short, infrequent and do not build up.

## A show
During pregnancy a plug of mucus sits in your cervix. It comes away just before or in early labour. It is sticky, jelly-like and pink because it holds a little blood.
It may come in one blob or in pieces. Labour may follow quickly or take a few days, and some people have no show. If you lose more blood than that, call your midwife or hospital straight away.

## Your waters breaking
Your waters will most likely break during labour, but they can break before it starts. You may feel a slow trickle or a sudden gush.
Amniotic fluid is clear and pale. Use a period pad, not a tampon, so your midwife can check the colour. Tell your midwife straight away if the fluid is smelly or coloured, or if you are losing blood.
Most people go into labour within 24 hours of their waters breaking. If you do not, you will be offered an induction because there is a small increased risk of infection.

## The early stage
The start of labour is called the latent phase. Your cervix softens and thins, and starts to open. It can take hours, or sometimes days, and you will probably be advised to stay at home.
Stay upright and gently active in the day, and rest at night if you can. Eat and drink. Breathing, massage, a warm bath or shower and paracetamol can help.
Labour is called established when your cervix is about 4 cm open and contractions are stronger and more regular.

## When to call
Call your midwife or maternity unit if you think you are in labour, or if contractions come every 5 minutes or more often. You can also call if you are unsure or worried about anything.
Call urgently if your waters break, you have vaginal bleeding, your baby moves less, you are under 37 weeks, a contraction lasts longer than 2 minutes, or you have 6 or more contractions in 10 minutes. Do not wait until morning.
Call 999 if you think your baby is coming now and you have a strong urge to push. If you cannot reach your midwife or unit, call 111.

## When to call your midwife
- Contractions every 5 minutes or closer
- Your waters break
- Bleeding from your vagina
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Under 37 weeks and you think you are in labour
- A contraction lasts over 2 minutes, or 6 or more in 10 minutes

## Questions
Q: How will I know it is real labour?
A: Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together, and do not ease when you rest or change position. If you are unsure, call your midwife or maternity unit.
Q: Should I go to hospital straight away?
A: Not usually. In early labour you will probably be advised to stay at home. Call first and they will tell you when to come in.
Q: What if my waters break but there are no contractions?
A: Call your midwife. Most people go into labour within 24 hours. If you do not, you will be offered an induction.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance on signs of labour and NICE intrapartum care guidance.
Sources: Signs that labour has begun (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/signs-that-labour-has-begun/); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/)

---

# Best positions for labour and birth
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/labour-positions/
Stage: Birth

How you move in labour can change how it feels. These are simple positions to try, and why they help.

## In short
- Stay upright: Standing, walking and leaning on a partner use gravity and can help baby move down.
- Use a birth ball: Sitting and rocking on a ball can ease backache and keep your hips loose.
- Hands and knees: Kneeling on all fours can help if you have backache.
- Change often: Moving and changing position can help. Do what feels right for you.

## Why move
On TV people give birth lying on their backs. That is not always the best position and may slow labour down.
Moving around, staying upright and changing position can increase your chance of a shorter labour, help you feel less pain, lead to fewer interventions including a lower chance of caesarean birth, and make you feel more in control.
Most people feel a need to move rather than keep still. Try to walk around in the first stage if you can.

## Positions to try
Sit leaning on a table, straddle a chair or toilet facing the back, or stand leaning on a bed, a table or your birth partner.
Kneel on the floor cradling a birth ball, or kneel on all fours. All fours can help if you have backache.
Rock, sit or gently bounce on a birth ball. Try a lunge with one knee bent, standing, kneeling or lying on your side. Squat if you have practised it.
If you get tired or contractions get stronger, shift your weight from foot to foot or rock your pelvis. Rest when you need to.

## In the pushing stage
In the second stage you may want to sit, lie on your side, stand, kneel or squat, though squatting may be hard if you are not used to it. Try some of these before labour.
Finding a comfortable upright position can help shorten the time you push for, and reduce your chance of an episiotomy and assisted birth.
If you had a lot of backache in labour, kneeling on all fours may help.

## Touch and water
Massage and soothing touch can help release oxytocin, the hormone that helps labour progress, and endorphins, your natural pain relief.
A birth pool can make changing position easier. Labouring in water is only advised if you and your baby are healthy and your pregnancy is low risk. If you have had opioid pain relief such as diamorphine, wait for it to wear off before getting in.

## If you have an epidural
An epidural can limit movement, partly because of your legs but mostly because of closer monitoring and the drip. Your midwife should still help you into comfortable upright positions in the first stage if you can manage it.
It also raises the chance of needing help to give birth, though less with modern epidurals. If it is your first baby and you find it hard to stay upright, lying on your side in the second stage may help avoid an assisted birth.

## Questions
Q: What is the best position for labour?
A: There is no single best one. Do what feels right and keep changing. Upright and moving positions are generally helpful.
Q: Can I move with an epidural?
A: Movement is more limited, but your midwife should still help you find comfortable upright positions in the first stage if you can manage it.

Evidence: Based on the Cochrane review of positions in the first stage of labour and NICE intrapartum care guidance.
Sources: Movement and positions during labour (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/movement-and-positions-during-labour); The stages of labour and birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/the-stages-of-labour-and-birth/)

---

# Water birth: what the research says
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/water-birth/
Stage: Birth

Warm water can help you relax and move freely in labour, and many birth centres and hospitals have a pool. This guide covers what the research found and how to ask for one.

## In short
- Why water helps: Warm water supports your weight and can ease pain. Some people need less other pain relief.
- What the research found: Research suggests labour in water is safe with a low-risk pregnancy. Babies’ health looks similar to birth out of water.
- Who it suits: Usually people with a healthy, low-risk pregnancy. Your midwife will tell you if it suits you.
- Plan ahead: Ask early if your birth place has a pool, and what happens if it is in use.

## What a water birth is
A water birth means labouring or giving birth in a deep bath or birthing pool.
Water can help with pain and many people find it more relaxing. It supports your weight so you can move more easily and feel more in control.

## Who can have one
It is an option if your pregnancy is low risk and your midwife or doctor thinks it is safe for you and your baby. Tell your midwife early.
It is generally not advised if your baby is breech, you are having twins or triplets, your baby is under 37 weeks or has passed meconium, or you have an infection, a high temperature or bleeding. It is also not advised if you have pre-eclampsia, your waters broke over 24 hours ago, you are on an induction drip, or you are at high risk of birth difficulties. Local guidance may differ.
The reason is that it may be hard to get you out of the pool safely in an emergency.

## Is it safe
Research suggests labour in water is safe if you have a low-risk pregnancy and can use a pool. Newborn infection and umbilical cord tears after water birth are very rare and can usually be treated.
There is not enough research to say whether water birth is safer or less safe than birth out of water. So far, babies’ health, including the chance of infection, looks similar.
Drowning is very unlikely. A baby born in water behaves as if still in the womb until they take their first breath of air.

## The advantages
Warm water can relax, soothe and comfort you. You can try different positions, and gravity helps your baby move down when you are upright.
It can lower your blood pressure and anxiety, help back pain and ease the feeling of pressure when you are fully dilated.

## The downsides
You cannot have an epidural, and you cannot have opiates such as pethidine for about 2 to 3 hours before getting in. You cannot use a TENS machine in the pool because of the danger of electrocution.
The effect on your baby’s temperature is unclear, so your midwife checks the water often. It is uncertain whether water affects the risk or severity of perineal tears. You may need to leave the pool if there is a complication.
A pool may not be free if your unit is busy. The NHS says the water is kept at a comfortable temperature, not above 37.5°C.

## Questions
Q: Can I change my mind about a water birth?
A: Yes. You can change your mind at any time, in or out of the water.
Q: Can I have an epidural in the pool?
A: No. You also cannot have opiates like pethidine for 2 to 3 hours before getting in.

Evidence: Based on the POOL cohort study (UK) and NHS guidance on water birth.
Sources: How to prepare for a water birth (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/where-can-i-give-birth/how-prepare-water-birth); Movement and positions during labour (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/movement-and-positions-during-labour); Pain relief in labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/pain-relief-in-labour/)

# What a doula does, and whether you need one
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/doula/
Stage: Birth

A doula is a trained birth companion. They give no medical care. They stay with you, help you feel steady and help you speak up for what you want.

## In short
- Before birth: Talks through your wishes, your fears and your birth plan with you.
- In labour: Stays with you the whole time. Helps with positions, breathing, touch and reassurance.
- After birth: Some doulas visit in the first weeks to help with feeding and rest.
- What the research found: People with continuous support in labour are less likely to have an assisted birth, a caesarean or a longer labour.

## What a doula is
A doula supports you one-to-one through pregnancy, labour and birth, or after your baby arrives. They offer practical and emotional support wherever and however you give birth.
They do not have to be medically trained and cannot replace the clinical care of your midwife or doctor. They give extra support and can help you find balanced information.

## What they can do
Birth doulas meet you in pregnancy, help with your birth plan, answer questions, and support you in labour whether you plan a caesarean, home birth or water birth.
Postnatal doulas help with practical and emotional support, confidence in caring for your baby and breastfeeding.

## Does it help
People who have continuous support in labour and birth are less likely to have an assisted birth, a caesarean, pain relief or a longer labour.
There is also some evidence that doula support improves the birth experience and your baby’s wellbeing just after birth.
A doula can speak up for you, which may help if you are anxious or have cultural or religious needs. They may also help if you are Black or Black Mixed Heritage and worry about not being listened to.

## Cost and training
Costs vary a lot, by where they work, their experience and what is included. Ask each doula directly.
You may be able to get free support through charities. Doula UK helps people who are disadvantaged or vulnerable, and you need to be referred by a healthcare professional or social worker.
There is no national regulation. Not all doulas are insured and some have no training, so ask about both.

## Finding one
NCT doulas have completed a 9-month course and have professional insurance. Doula UK members have completed an approved preparation course. You can also ask your midwife about local doulas.
Many doulas offer a first meeting, so you can see whether you are a good fit.

## Questions
Q: Is a doula a replacement for my midwife?
A: No. A doula gives extra support but cannot replace the clinical care of your midwife or doctor.
Q: Can I get a doula for free?
A: Sometimes. Doula UK and some local charities support people who are disadvantaged or vulnerable. You usually need a referral.

Evidence: Based on the Cochrane review of continuous support for women during childbirth.
Sources: What is a doula? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/labour-and-birth-faqs/what-doula)

---

# Birth partner guide: how to help in labour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/birth-partner/
Stage: Birth

A good birth partner helps you feel safe and heard. This guide covers what to do and what to say, in plain steps.

## In short
- Know the plan: Read the birth plan together. You can speak up for the wishes when your partner is busy coping.
- Comfort measures: Offer water, massage, a cool cloth, a change of position and kind words.
- Stay steady: Slow breathing from you helps. It is fine to ask the midwife to explain what is happening.
- Look after yourself: Eat, drink and take short breaks. You will be needed after the birth too.

## Choosing who
A birth partner gives practical and emotional support in labour. Having someone with you can help you cope better with contractions and help labour go more smoothly.
It can be your baby’s parent, your partner, a close friend or relative, or a doula. Choose the person you trust most and who you feel will support you best. Do not worry about hurting feelings.

## What makes a good one
Someone steady under pressure who is sensitive to your needs, can help you move around, explains what is going on clearly, and supports your breathing and relaxation.
They should be able to ask for help or speak up for you, and take control if you need them to.

## How many
You can have more than one. At home you can have as many as you like. In hospital or a birth centre there may be a limit, and there may be one for a caesarean too. Ask your midwife in pregnancy.
A carer or interpreter should not count as a birth partner.

## Getting ready together
Talk well in advance about how you want them to help. Share your hopes and fears, show them your birth plan, and show them any relaxation methods or TENS pads you plan to use.
Antenatal classes with your birth partner can help you both feel prepared.
Remind them you can change your mind at any point. Only you can consent to treatment, but they can pass on your wishes to staff if you need them to.

## After the birth
In hospital there may be a limit on how long a birth partner can stay. Some can stay overnight, others must leave and return in visiting hours.
If you are worried about your partner leaving, talk to a nurse on your ward and explain why. They may be able to arrange for them to stay longer.

## Questions
Q: Can I have more than one birth partner?
A: Yes. At home there is no limit. In hospital or a birth centre there may be one, so ask your midwife.
Q: Can my partner stay after the birth?
A: It depends on your hospital’s policy. Ask a nurse on the ward if you want them to stay longer.

Evidence: Based on NHS guidance for birth partners and Cochrane evidence on continuous support in labour.
Sources: Who can be my birth partner? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/labour-and-birth-faqs/who-can-be-my-birth-partner)

---

# Breathing and relaxation for labour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/hypnobirthing-breathing/
Stage: Birth

Slow, steady breathing can help you cope with contractions. You can practise these techniques at home in a few minutes a day.

## In short
- Slow breathing: Breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth. It may help you feel more in control.
- Relaxation: Soften your jaw, shoulders and hands. A relaxed body often means a more relaxed mind.
- Practise often: A few minutes a day in pregnancy makes it easier to use when labour comes.
- The evidence: Some research shows hypnobirthing can reduce fear and pain, though not all studies agree. You can use it with other pain relief.

## What it is
Hypnobirthing is a mix of visualisation, relaxation and deep breathing. The aim is to help you feel more relaxed, more in control and better able to cope with labour pain.
You can use it with any other pain relief, and add it to your birth plan.

## The techniques
Controlled breathing: in through your nose and out through your mouth. It may help you feel more in control and cope without medical pain relief.
Visualisation: picture something pleasant, such as a flower opening with each wave, or holding your baby skin to skin.
Deep relaxation: a kind of meditation that helps you focus on your body and baby and block out noise around you.
Positive words, such as “each surge brings me closer to meeting my baby”, can help too.

## Does it work
Tommy’s says research has shown hypnobirthing can reduce fear and pain and give you more sense of control. It may help anxiety and reduce medical interventions, though not all studies have found this.
The NHS says most complementary methods, including hypnosis, are not proven to give effective pain relief. If you want to try them, talk to your midwife first.
Practising it does not mean labour will go smoothly. Learning to stay relaxed may still help if things do not go to plan.

## How to practise
Some people practise a few times a day, others 2 to 3 times a week. Fit it in while you are pregnant so it works for you in labour.
You can learn from a class, a book, an app or free online courses. In some areas NHS midwives run classes. Most private courses cost money.

## One thing to tell your midwife
Hypnobirthing can be so relaxing that a midwife may think you are at an earlier stage than you are. Say clearly that you are using it when you phone or arrive.

## Questions
Q: Is hypnobirthing proven to work?
A: Tommy’s says research shows it can reduce fear and pain, though not all studies agree. The NHS says most complementary methods are not proven for pain. It does not replace medical pain relief if you want it.
Q: Can I use it with an epidural or gas and air?
A: Yes. You can use hypnobirthing techniques alongside any other pain relief.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane reviews of relaxation and antenatal education, and NHS guidance on coping with labour.
Sources: What is hypnobirthing? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/pain-relief/hypnobirthing); Pain relief in labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/pain-relief-in-labour/)

---

# How to write a birth plan
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/birth-plan/
Stage: Birth

A birth plan is a short note on what matters to you in labour. Keep it to one page that your team can read in a minute.

## In short
- Keep it short: One page is enough. Use plain words and put your most important wishes first.
- What to include: Who you want with you, positions and movement, pain relief wishes, and your feeding plan.
- Plan for change: Birth can go a different way. Add what you would want if plans change, such as skin-to-skin after a caesarean.
- Share it early: Talk it through with your midwife before labour and bring a copy.

## What a birth plan is
A birth plan is a written record of what you would like to happen in labour and after the birth. It can also include things you want to avoid.
You do not need one. But writing one can help you understand your choices even if you do not use it in the end.

## How to make one
You do not need a special form. A few points on a sheet of paper is fine, or you can use a template from the NHS. Put a few copies in your hospital bag.
Your midwife can answer questions, tell you about options in your area and help you work out what you want.

## What to include
Who you want as your birth partner, where you want to give birth, positions you would like to try, and what pain relief you want.
Whether you want delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin contact straight away, and how you plan to feed your baby.
How you feel about an episiotomy, ventouse or forceps, and fetal monitoring. Any special needs, like an interpreter or religious customs.
Share it with your birth partner so they can support you better.

## If you are having a caesarean
You can still have a plan. You may want the screen lowered to see your baby’s birth, or a quiet theatre so your voice is the first your baby hears.
If you are not planning a caesarean, it may still be worth adding a section in case you need one. Unless it is a real emergency there should be time to follow your choices.

## After the birth
You will be offered vitamin K for your baby, to help prevent a rare bleeding disorder. You can say in your plan if you would prefer it by mouth, which needs more doses.
Delayed cord clamping should happen automatically, but it can help to mention it.

## Staying flexible
Things do not always go to plan. A pool may not be free, or you may need to move to hospital during a home birth. Do not worry about covering every possibility.
You can change your mind at any time, even in labour. Keep an open mind, because you may want more pain relief than you planned.

## Questions
Q: Do I have to write a birth plan?
A: No. There is no need unless you want one.
Q: Can I change it during labour?
A: Yes. You can change your mind at any time, including during labour.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on shared decision making in maternity care.
Sources: Making your birth plan (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/making-your-birth-plan); What happens straight after the birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/what-happens-straight-after/); Pain relief in labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/pain-relief-in-labour/)

---

# Where to give birth: home, birth centre or hospital
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/home-birth-or-hospital/
Stage: Birth

You have a choice about where to give birth. Each place is explained fairly, so you can decide with your midwife.

## In short
- At home: With a midwife present. Usually only advised for a straightforward pregnancy. You can move to hospital at any time.
- Midwife-led unit: A homelike setting with midwives. Medical help is nearby or on site.
- Hospital: Best if you or baby need extra care. Doctors and pain relief such as epidural are available.
- Ask your midwife: Your history matters. Ask what is safest and what is available near you.

## Your choices
You can give birth at home, in a midwife-led unit or birth centre, or in hospital. Where you give birth is up to you, and you can change your mind at any point in pregnancy.
If your pregnancy is high risk or you have certain conditions, it is safest to give birth in hospital, where specialists are available.
You are free to choose any maternity service if you are willing to travel. Ask your midwife about visiting local units.

## Home birth
It is usually recommended only if you have a straightforward pregnancy and you and your baby are well. A midwife stays with you during labour and arranges a move to hospital if needed.
If it is your first baby, a home birth slightly increases the risk of serious problems for the baby, from 5 in 1,000 for a hospital birth to 9 in 1,000. If you have had a baby before, a planned home birth is as safe as hospital or a midwife-led unit.
The benefits include familiar surroundings, not having to interrupt labour to travel, and, if your pregnancy is low risk, a lower chance of forceps or ventouse.
You cannot have an epidural at home, but you can have gas and air, a warm bath or pool, TENS and relaxation. Some NHS trusts do not offer pethidine at home.

## Midwife-led unit or birth centre
These are more homely than a hospital ward. Some are part of a hospital and some are separate, with no immediate obstetric or anaesthetic care.
If low risk, you are less likely to need forceps or ventouse. In a separate unit you cannot have an epidural, so ask whether yours is attached to a hospital.

## Hospital
Most births happen in an NHS hospital maternity unit. You get direct access to obstetricians, anaesthetists for epidurals, and newborn specialists.
You are more likely to have an epidural, an episiotomy or a forceps or ventouse delivery in hospital. You may also see a different midwife from the one in pregnancy.

## Transferring to hospital
You can change your mind and go to hospital at any time, even in labour.
You will need to move if labour is not progressing or if there are complications, for example bleeding, a baby who has passed meconium, or waters that broke 18 or more hours before labour.
Ask your midwife how long a transfer would take, which hospital you would go to, and whether a midwife will be with you the whole time.

## If you have a risk factor
You may be advised to give birth in hospital if you have pre-eclampsia or high blood pressure, diabetes, a high BMI, abnormal scans, a previous caesarean, a breech baby, a multiple pregnancy, or a previous premature birth.
Your midwife or doctor will explain why they think hospital is safer.

## Questions
Q: Is a home birth safe?
A: Giving birth is generally safe wherever you choose. For a first baby, home birth slightly raises the risk of serious problems for the baby. For second and later babies, a planned home birth is as safe as hospital.
Q: Can I change my mind in labour?
A: Yes. You can go to hospital at any time, and your midwife can organise it.

Evidence: Based on NICE intrapartum care guidance and the Birthplace in England study.
Sources: Where to give birth: the options (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/where-to-give-birth-the-options/); Having a home birth (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/where-can-i-give-birth/having-home-birth)

---

# Hospital bag checklist: what to pack for labour and after
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/hospital-bag/
Stage: Birth

A packed bag takes one worry away. This is a short list, so you bring only what you need.

## In short
- For labour: Your birth plan and notes, comfortable clothes, snacks and drinks, a lip balm and a phone charger.
- For after: Loose clothes, comfy underwear, maternity pads, toiletries and a nursing bra if you plan to breastfeed.
- For baby: A few sleepsuits, vests, a hat, nappies and a car seat if you are driving home.
- When to pack: Pack a few weeks early, and by 37 weeks at the latest.

## When to pack
Pack a bag even if you plan a home birth, in case you need to go in. Have everything ready by 37 weeks at the latest.
You might give birth on your due date, but do not bet on it. Pack for at least a couple of days.

## For labour
Your antenatal notes. Keep them with you at all times in the last months.
One or two comfy nighties or big t-shirts. Labour rooms are warm. A comfy change of clothes.
Drinks and snacks for you and your birth partner, something to read or listen to, a face cloth and a water spray, lip balm, hair bobbles, and a pillow from home.
Phone, headphones and chargers, bank cards and change for the car park, toiletries, your medications, and a TENS machine if you want one.

## For after the birth
Front-opening nighties or loose shirts, a light dressing gown and slippers, and a couple of packets of maternity pads. Do not use tampons.
5 or 6 pairs of knickers, 2 or 3 nursing or comfy bras, breast pads, and nipple cream. Clothes to come home in that are comfy and loose.
If you are bottle-feeding, sterile bottles, teats and formula.

## For your baby
Up to 5 sleepsuits and vests, a pack of newborn nappies, cotton wool and water for cleaning, and a baby blanket or shawl. Avoid wipes for the first few weeks.
Clothes to come home in, such as a hat, scratch mittens, socks and a pram suit if it is cold.
You will also need a car seat to bring your baby home.

## Tips
You may prefer two bags, one for labour and one for after. Put them in a wheeled suitcase.
Pack a nappy, hat and vest at the top so your birth partner can find them fast.
Your hospital can usually provide basics like towels and blankets. Ask your midwife for a list specific to your unit.

## Questions
Q: When should I pack my bag?
A: A few weeks early, and by 37 weeks at the latest.
Q: Do I need a bag for a home birth?
A: Yes. Have one ready in case you need to go in.

Evidence: Based on NHS suggestions for what to pack for labour and birth.
Sources: Packing your bag for labour and birth (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/packing-hospital-bag)

# Do dates help labour? What the research says
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/dates-late-pregnancy/
Stage: Birth

Many people hear that eating dates near the end of pregnancy helps labour. This guide covers what the studies found and how strong the proof is.

## In short
- What people do: Some people eat dates in the weeks before their due date, as a snack.
- What studies found: There is some evidence dates may help, but bigger and better studies are needed.
- Check first: There are no proven ways to safely start labour at home. Ask your midwife before trying anything.
- Keep it simple: Dates are a food, not a treatment. They do not replace care from your midwife.

## Waiting past 40 weeks
Many babies arrive after their due date. At your 38 and 40 week appointments your midwife talks through your choices if you are still pregnant after 40 weeks.
If labour has not started by 41 weeks, induction is offered because the risk of stillbirth or problems for the baby is higher.

## The truth about home remedies
There is not enough strong evidence that home remedies start labour, and some may not be safe. Always ask your midwife first.
The NHS says there are no proven ways of starting labour yourself at home. There is also no safety information on herbal supplements.

## Dates
There is a theory that eating dates for a few weeks before your due date may help your cervix open. Dates contain prostaglandins, which may play a part in starting labour.
There is some evidence they can help, but bigger and better studies are needed to be sure. A handful of dates is a healthy snack either way.

## Walking and other ideas
There is a small amount of evidence that walking for 30 minutes, three times a week, may increase your chance of going into labour. Walk only as far and as fast as is comfortable.
There is little to suggest acupuncture can trigger labour. If you try it, use a fully qualified practitioner who is used to pregnancy.
There is no proof that spicy food works, and no evidence that sex starts labour. Sex will not cause harm, but avoid it if your waters have broken.

## Raspberry leaf tea
Health professionals do not suggest raspberry leaf tea for getting labour going. Experts are unsure whether it works or how safe it is.
It may not be safe if you have had a caesarean in the last 2 years or plan one, have high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia, had premature labour before, are carrying more than one baby or a breech baby, or take antidepressants. Check with your midwife first.

## What your midwife can offer
From 39 weeks you can be offered a membrane sweep to bring on labour. If your pregnancy goes past 42 weeks and you decide against induction, you should be offered more monitoring.
Use the waiting time to rest and do things you enjoy.

## When to call your midwife
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Your waters break
- Vaginal bleeding
- You are past your due date and want to talk through your options

## Questions
Q: Do dates really bring on labour?
A: There is some evidence they may help, but bigger studies are needed. They are a healthy snack, but not a proven way to start labour.
Q: Is raspberry leaf tea safe?
A: Experts are unsure. Talk to your midwife before trying it, as it is not safe in some situations.

Evidence: Based on small clinical trials and reviews of date fruit in late pregnancy. The evidence is limited and more research is needed.
Sources: Antenatal care and appointments (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/your-pregnancy-care/your-antenatal-care-and-appointments/); Inducing labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/inducing-labour/); Can anything bring labour on? (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/labour-and-birth-faqs/can-anything-bring-labour)

# Tear prevention: perineal massage and what else helps
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/perineal-tear-prevention/
Stage: Birth

Many people worry about tearing. This guide covers what the research says helps and how to talk about it with your midwife.

## In short
- Perineal massage: From 35 weeks, perineal massage has been shown to reduce the risk of tears, especially in a first birth.
- In labour: You can ask your midwife to support your perineum as your baby is born. This lowers the risk of a deeper tear.
- Positions: A kneeling or all-fours position may reduce how severe tearing is.
- Healing: Keep clean and dry, rest, and use pain relief. Call if pain worsens or the wound smells.

## How common tears are
Up to 9 in 10 first-time mothers who have a vaginal birth will have some sort of tear, graze or episiotomy.
Most tears heal within 6 weeks with no long-term problems. About 6 in 100 first-time mothers, and 2 in 100 who have given birth vaginally before, have a deeper tear involving the anal muscle. These are repaired in an operating theatre.

## What may help
A kneeling or all-fours birthing position may be beneficial and may reduce how severe tearing is.
You can ask your midwife to support your perineum as your baby is born. This “hands-on” birth reduces the risk of a deeper tear.
From 35 weeks you may choose to try perineal massage until your baby arrives. It has been shown to reduce the risk of tears and is most helpful for first-time mothers.

## How to do perineal massage
Use a lubricant such as vitamin E oil, almond oil or olive oil.
Hold one or both thumbs just inside the vagina for about a minute until you feel a stretch. Keep breathing.
Gently massage the lower half of the vagina in a U-shaped movement for 2 to 3 minutes. Do this 2 to 3 times, daily or when you can. Your partner can help.

## Episiotomy
An episiotomy is a cut to make the opening wider. In England it is not done routinely.
NICE says it might be done if your baby is in distress and needs to be born quickly, if forceps or ventouse are needed, or if there is a risk of a tear to the anus. Your midwife or doctor will talk it through with you.

## After the birth
If you have a tear or an episiotomy you will probably need dissolvable stitches. Stitches should heal within about a month.
Paracetamol is safe while breastfeeding. A wrapped ice pack, airing the stitches and pouring warm water over the area as you pee can help. Pain usually does not last longer than 2 to 3 weeks.
Pelvic floor exercises help healing and ease pressure on the area. A midwife can show you how.

## When to call your midwife
- Your stitches get more painful
- Smelly discharge
- Red, swollen skin around the cut or tear
- Pain after a tear lasts longer than 2 to 3 weeks

## Questions
Q: Does perineal massage work?
A: The RCOG says it has been shown to reduce the risk of tears when done from 35 weeks, especially for first-time mothers. It is your choice.
Q: Will I need stitches?
A: Small tears and grazes are often left without stitches. A larger tear or an episiotomy needs dissolvable stitches, which heal within about a month.

Evidence: Based on Cochrane review of perineal massage and RCOG guidance on tears.
Sources: Episiotomy and perineal tears (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/episiotomy-and-perineal-tears/); Perineal tears during childbirth (https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/perineal-tears-during-childbirth-patient-information-poster/)
