# Pain relief in labour: every option compared
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/pain-relief-in-labour/
Stage: Birth

There is no right or wrong way to cope with labour. Every option is covered fairly, so you can choose and change your mind.

## In short
- Without medicine: Warm water, massage, movement, breathing and a quiet room can all help.
- TENS and gas and air: Gas and air takes 15 to 20 seconds to work and you control it yourself. TENS is most useful in early labour.
- Injections: Pethidine or similar can take the edge off pain but may make you or baby drowsy.
- Epidural: In most cases an epidural gives complete pain relief. It can lengthen the pushing stage, so forceps or ventouse may be needed.

## Help yourself first
You are likely to cope better if you learn about labour, learn to relax and breathe deeply, and keep moving. Try kneeling, walking or rocking.
A support person, a massage, a warm bath and paracetamol in early labour can all help. Keep an open mind, because you may want more pain relief than you planned.

## Gas and air
Gas and air is oxygen and nitrous oxide. It does not remove all the pain but makes it more bearable, and you control it yourself. It takes 15 to 20 seconds to work, so breathe it in as a contraction begins.
It can make you light-headed, sick or sleepy. If it does, you can stop. Using it for more than 24 hours can lower your vitamin B12.

## Injections
Pethidine or, less often, diamorphine, is injected into your thigh or buttock. It takes about 20 minutes to work and lasts 2 to 4 hours, so it is not recommended close to the pushing stage.
It can make you woozy and sick. Given too close to the birth it can affect your baby’s breathing, and it can interfere with the first feed.

## Epidural
An epidural numbs the nerves that carry pain from the birth canal. In most cases it gives complete pain relief. Only an anaesthetist can give one, so it is not available at home.
It takes about 10 minutes to set up and 10 to 15 more to work. Your contractions and baby’s heart rate are monitored continuously.
Side effects can include heavy legs, difficulty peeing, and a longer pushing stage, which can mean forceps or ventouse are needed. A headache happens in about 1 in 100 cases. Epidurals do not cause long-term backache.

## Remifentanil, water and TENS
Remifentanil goes into a vein and you control it with a button. It works quickly and wears off in minutes. It can make you sleepy, sick or itchy, and may briefly affect your baby’s breathing.
Water can help you relax and make contractions seem less painful. The water is kept at a comfortable temperature, not above 37.5°C.
TENS has not been shown to work in active labour. It is probably most helpful in early labour, especially for lower back pain, and has no known side effects.

## Other methods
Acupuncture, aromatherapy, homeopathy, hypnosis, massage and reflexology are options, but most are not proven to give effective pain relief. Most hospitals do not offer them.
If you want to try them, talk to your midwife first and choose a properly trained practitioner.

## Questions
Q: Can I change my mind?
A: Yes. Write your wishes in your birth plan but keep an open mind. You can ask for more pain relief at any point.
Q: Will an epidural slow my labour?
A: It can lengthen the pushing stage, so forceps or ventouse may be needed. Your midwife may wait longer before you push to lower that chance.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on pain relief in labour.
Sources: Pain relief in labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/pain-relief-in-labour/)

---

# Induction of labour: why, how and what to ask
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/induction-of-labour/
Stage: Birth

Induction means starting labour with medical help. This guide covers why it is offered, how it works and the questions worth asking.

## In short
- Why it is offered: Common reasons are going past your due date, your waters breaking without labour, or a health concern for you or baby.
- How it works: You are first offered a membrane sweep. Induction itself uses hormones or a small balloon, and happens in hospital.
- It can take time: Induction often takes longer than labour that starts on its own. Bring things to pass the time.
- Ask questions: Ask what the risks are of both inducing and waiting, and what your other choices are.

## What induction is
Induction starts labour artificially. It is common if your baby is overdue or there is a risk to you or your baby’s health.
It is usually planned in advance, and it is your choice whether to have it.

## Why you might be offered it
If you have not gone into labour by 41 weeks, induction is offered because the risk of stillbirth or problems for the baby is higher.
If your pregnancy lasts longer than 42 weeks and you decide not to be induced, you should be offered increased monitoring.
If your waters break more than 24 hours before labour starts, there is a higher risk of infection. After 34 weeks you can choose induction or expectant management, where you are monitored and the pregnancy progresses naturally while it is safe.
You may also be offered it for a health condition such as diabetes, high blood pressure or intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, or if your baby is not growing well.

## A membrane sweep first
Before induction you will be offered a membrane sweep, usually after 39 weeks. Your midwife or doctor sweeps a finger around your cervix to separate the membranes, which releases hormones that may start labour.
It can be uncomfortable or painful, with some cramping and bleeding afterwards.

## How it is done
Induction is always done in a hospital maternity unit. There are 2 main ways: hormones as a vaginal tablet or gel, or a device such as a small water balloon or a sponge to widen your cervix. You will usually be offered hormones first.
It usually takes many hours to start working. Sometimes a hormone drip or breaking your waters is needed to speed things up.

## What to expect
Induced labour is usually more painful than labour that starts alone, and you are more likely to have an assisted delivery with forceps or ventouse.
Your pain relief options are not restricted by being induced. You can still have an epidural or a water birth.
Induction does not always work. You may be offered another method or a caesarean, or you may wait a few hours and be assessed again.

## Natural ways to start labour
There are no proven ways to start labour yourself at home. There is no evidence that hot baths, certain foods or drinks, sex or herbal supplements work.
There is no safety information on herbal supplements, and they could harm you or your baby. Sex will not cause harm, but avoid it if your waters have broken.

## When to call your midwife
- Your waters break
- Your baby moves less than usual
- Vaginal bleeding
- You have not gone into labour by 41 weeks. Ask about your options

## Questions
Q: Do I have to be induced?
A: No. It is your choice. If you decide against it after 42 weeks, you should be offered increased monitoring of your baby.
Q: Does a membrane sweep hurt?
A: Some people find it uncomfortable or painful, and you may have cramping or light bleeding afterwards.
Q: Can I bring on labour myself?
A: There are no proven ways to safely do this at home. Ask your midwife before trying anything.

Evidence: Based on NICE guideline on inducing labour and NHS guidance.
Sources: Inducing labour (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/inducing-labour/)

---

# Caesarean birth: planned and unplanned
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/caesarean-birth/
Stage: Birth

A caesarean is a real birth. This guide covers why one may be advised, what happens and how you can still make it feel like yours.

## In short
- Why it happens: Reasons include baby’s position, a health concern or labour not progressing. Some are planned and some are not.
- What happens: You are usually awake with a spinal block. The operation is quick, and your birth partner can often be there.
- Make it yours: Ask about skin-to-skin in theatre, delayed cord clamping and your feeding plan.
- Recovery: Rest, gentle walking and pain relief help. Call your midwife about a fever, a wound that looks red or smells, or heavy bleeding.

## What a caesarean is
A caesarean is an operation to deliver your baby through a cut in your tummy and womb. It is a major operation with risks, so it is usually done only if it is the safest option for you and your baby.
About 1 in 4 women who give birth in the UK have one, and most of those are emergency caesareans.

## Planned or emergency
A planned caesarean is usually done from 39 weeks, because babies born earlier are more likely to need help with breathing.
Reasons include a breech baby, a low-lying placenta, pre-eclampsia, certain infections, twins in a difficult position, or more than two babies.
An emergency caesarean may be needed if labour is not progressing, there is heavy bleeding, or your baby is not getting enough oxygen. Even then there is often time to decide, and your team will explain your options.
You can also ask for a caesarean with no medical reason. You will be offered a chance to talk about the benefits and risks, and support if you are anxious about birth.

## What happens
The week before, you have a pre-op appointment with a blood test and medicines to take. You stop eating and drinking a few hours before.
Most are done with a spinal or epidural, so you are awake but numb from the waist down. A screen is placed across your tummy. Your birth partner can usually be with you.
A cut about 10 to 20 cm is made, usually just below the bikini line. Your baby is delivered in about 5 to 10 minutes and you may feel tugging. The whole operation takes about 40 to 50 minutes.
If your baby is well, you can see and hold them straight away. You are given oxytocin to help your womb contract and reduce bleeding.
A general anaesthetic is used occasionally, for example if your baby needs to be delivered more quickly. Your birth partner is not normally present then.

## Risks
A caesarean is generally very safe, but risks to you include wound infection and infection of the womb lining (both common), excessive bleeding, blood clots and bladder damage (rarer). You are given antibiotics beforehand to lower infection.
For your baby, a small cut to the skin and breathing difficulties are the most common. Breathing problems are most often seen in babies born before 39 weeks and usually improve in a few days.
Future pregnancies are usually fine. Most people who have had a caesarean can safely have a vaginal birth next time, though some are advised to have another caesarean.

## Recovery
Most people go home 1 to 2 days after. You are given painkillers, and encouraged to get up and move as soon as possible. The catheter usually comes out after 12 to 18 hours.
Clean and dry the wound daily, wear loose clothes and cotton underwear, and use paracetamol or ibuprofen if sore. Avoid aspirin while breastfeeding. Use pads, not tampons, for bleeding.
You may not be able to drive, exercise, carry more than your baby or have sex for about 6 weeks. Try to walk daily to lower the risk of blood clots.

## Making it yours
You can still have a birth plan. You might ask for the screen to be lowered to see your baby, or a quiet theatre.
You can still have delayed cord clamping, and help with breastfeeding afterwards.

## When to call your midwife
- Severe pain, or pain when peeing, or leaking urine
- Heavy vaginal bleeding
- Wound more red, painful or swollen, or pus or foul-smelling fluid
- A cough, shortness of breath, or swelling or pain in your lower leg

## Questions
Q: Will I be awake?
A: Usually yes. Most caesareans use a spinal or epidural so you are awake but numb from the waist down. A general anaesthetic is used only occasionally.
Q: Can I have a vaginal birth next time?
A: Most people who have had a caesarean can safely have a vaginal birth next time. Some are advised to have another caesarean. Talk it through with your midwife or doctor.
Q: How long does recovery take?
A: Most people go home after 1 to 2 days. You may need to take things easy for several weeks and avoid driving, exercise and heavy lifting for about 6 weeks.

Evidence: Based on NICE caesarean birth guideline and NHS guidance.
Sources: Caesarean section (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/caesarean-section/); Caesarean section: what happens (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/caesarean-section/what-happens/); Caesarean section: risks (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/caesarean-section/risks/); Caesarean section: recovery (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/caesarean-section/recovery/); C-sections: everything you need to know (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/caesarean-section/c-sections-everything-you-need-know); Making your birth plan (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/making-your-birth-plan); Delayed (optimal) cord clamping (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/delayed-cord-clamping-optimal)

---

# The first six weeks after birth: what to expect
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/after-birth/
Stage: After birth

The first weeks after birth bring a lot of change. Take them one day at a time: skin-to-skin, feeding, healing and how you feel.

## In short
- Skin-to-skin: Skin-to-skin right after birth helps bonding and can help feeding start.
- Feeding: Breast, bottle or both. Mia explains each and when to ask for help.
- Healing: Bleeding, stitches and tiredness are normal. Know the signs that need a call to your midwife.
- Your mood: Feeling low for a few days is common. If it lasts more than two weeks, talk to someone.

## Straight after
Skin-to-skin contact helps with bonding and with getting breastfeeding started. You can ask for your baby to be lifted onto you as soon as they are born, before the cord is cut.
Your baby will be dried and covered with a towel to keep warm while you cuddle. They may have some of your blood and vernix, the greasy white coating, on their skin.
Your baby is examined, weighed and given a name band. You are offered an injection of vitamin K for your baby to help prevent a rare bleeding disorder. If you prefer, they can have it by mouth with more doses.

## Stitches and bleeding
Small tears and grazes are often left to heal without stitches. A large tear or an episiotomy needs stitches, and you can keep cuddling your baby while it is done.
You are offered an injection of oxytocin as your baby is born to help prevent heavy bleeding.
You will bleed from the vagina for a few weeks, called lochia. It usually stops after 6 to 8 weeks but can last longer.

## Checks for your baby
Within 72 hours a paediatrician, midwife or neonatal nurse offers a full physical check. In the early days your midwife also checks for jaundice, infection of the cord or eyes, and thrush.
On day 5, or a few days later, you are offered the newborn blood spot (heel prick) test. Before 4 weeks you are offered a hearing screening test.
It is normal for babies to lose some weight in the first few days. Most regain their birth weight in the first 3 weeks.

## Checks for you
Staff check your temperature, pulse, blood pressure, breathing, bleeding, and that you can pee and poo. They feel your tummy to see your womb shrinking back. Some people feel tummy pain as it shrinks, especially when breastfeeding. That is normal.
Midwives agree a plan for home or clinic visits until your baby is about 10 days old. A health visitor sees you around 10 to 14 days.

## Feelings
You may feel a bit down, tearful or anxious in the first week. That is normal. If it starts later or lasts more than 2 weeks, it could be postnatal depression. Speak to your midwife, GP or health visitor as soon as you can.

## Feeding, sleep and rest
Breastfeed as often as your baby wants, sometimes every hour in the early days. Let your baby decide when they have had enough.
Put your baby on their back to sleep to lower the risk of SIDS. Sex can wait until you feel ready, but you can get pregnant from 21 days after birth, even before a period and even if you are breastfeeding.
Gentle exercise such as walking, stretches and pelvic floor exercises can help your body recover.

## When to call your midwife
- Sudden, very heavy bleeding, or you feel faint, dizzy or have a pounding heart. Call 999
- Temperature over 38°C, or bleeding that smells unusual
- Tummy pain that gets worse, or bleeding that gets heavier or has clots
- Pain between your vagina and anus that gets worse

## Questions
Q: How long will I bleed after birth?
A: Usually 6 to 8 weeks, sometimes longer. Speak to your midwife or GP if you are worried or if it gets heavier.
Q: When can I get pregnant again?
A: From 21 days after birth, even if you are breastfeeding and have not had a period. Talk to your midwife about contraception.

Evidence: Based on WHO recommendations on postnatal care and NHS guidance after birth.
Sources: What happens straight after the birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/what-happens-straight-after/); Early days (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/early-days/)

# Delayed cord clamping and the golden hour
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/delayed-cord-clamping/
Stage: After birth

The first minutes after birth matter. This guide explains cord clamping in plain words.

## In short
- Waiting helps: Waiting at least one minute before clamping lets more blood pass to baby and is advised for most births.
- Skin-to-skin: Holding baby on your chest keeps them warm and settled and helps feeding start.
- At the birth: You can still cut the cord yourself. Delayed clamping is also possible after a caesarean.
- If baby needs help: Sometimes the cord is cut sooner so baby can get care. Your team will tell you why.

## What it is
Delayed or optimal cord clamping means your midwife or doctor waits 1 to 5 minutes before cutting the cord. The cord should not be clamped earlier than 1 minute after birth.
For those minutes the cord keeps passing blood, oxygen and stem cells to your baby while they adjust to breathing air.

## Why it matters
Your baby gets a full volume of blood at birth. This gives higher iron levels until about 6 months, which helps growth and development.
It also gives more stem cells, which help growth and the immune system. There is good evidence that delayed clamping can prevent deaths in premature babies.

## What it looks like
The NHS suggests your baby is lifted onto you straight after birth, before the cord is cut, so you are close right away.
You or your birth partner can still cut the cord. Delayed clamping can also happen if you have help delivering the placenta, or if you have a caesarean, planned or emergency.
Delayed clamping should happen automatically, but it can help to mention it in your birth plan.

## When it may not happen
It is almost always recommended. Your team may clamp earlier if your baby needs to be treated quickly, for example for their heartbeat or breathing.
Rare reasons include heavy bleeding in the mother, a problem with the placenta such as placental abruption or placenta praevia, or a bleeding cord. Twins who share a placenta should not have delayed clamping.
If your baby needs help breathing, your team may be able to help without cutting the cord. Some units have equipment to do this.

## Questions
Q: How long is delayed cord clamping?
A: Between 1 and 5 minutes after birth. The cord should not be clamped before 1 minute.
Q: Can I have it with a caesarean?
A: Yes. Giving birth by caesarean does not in itself prevent delayed cord clamping.

Evidence: Based on WHO and NICE guidance on cord clamping and immediate skin-to-skin contact.
Sources: Delayed (optimal) cord clamping (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/delayed-cord-clamping-optimal); What happens straight after the birth (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/what-happens-straight-after/); Making your birth plan (https://www.tommys.org/pregnancy-information/giving-birth/making-your-birth-plan)

# Breastfeeding basics: latch, feeds and where to get help
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/breastfeeding-basics/
Stage: After birth

Feeding is a skill you and your baby learn together. These are the basics, and where to find help, whatever you choose.

## In short
- The first feed: Skin-to-skin soon after birth helps baby find the breast. Ask for help with the first feed.
- A good latch: Baby’s mouth wide open and chin touching your breast, with more dark skin above their top lip than below.
- How often: Newborns feed often, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Feed when baby shows early hunger signs.
- Ask for help: Pain, a baby who is not feeding or not having wet nappies need a call to your midwife or feeding specialist.

## Why people breastfeed
Breast milk gives your baby nutrition, protects them from infections and diseases, and is available whenever they need it. It also has health benefits for you.
It can lower your baby’s risk of infections, diarrhoea and vomiting, SIDS and obesity. For you, it lowers the risk of breast and ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, obesity and diabetes.
Any amount of breast milk helps, and the longer you breastfeed the greater the benefit. Nothing but breast milk is recommended for about the first 6 months. You do not have to decide until your baby is born.

## The first hours
Skin-to-skin straight after birth keeps your baby warm and settled, steadies their breathing, and is a great time for the first feed. You can still do it after a caesarean.
If skin-to-skin is delayed, for example if your baby needs special care, you can still bond and breastfeed.

## Your first milk
The first milk, called colostrum, is thick and golden yellow. It is very concentrated, so your baby only needs about a teaspoonful at each feed.
Around 2 to 4 days after birth your breasts become fuller as your milk comes in. Nearly all women make enough milk for their baby.

## How often
In the first week your baby may want to feed every 1 to 3 hours. As a rough guide, feed at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours in the first few weeks.
Feed as often and as long as your baby wants. You cannot overfeed a breastfed baby. Early hunger signs are restlessness, sucking fists, murmuring and turning their head with an open mouth.
Feed at night, because you make more of the hormone that builds supply then. In the early weeks, formula top-ups or a dummy can lower your supply.

## Positioning and latch
Breastfeeding is a skill you and your baby learn together. Check that you are comfortable, your baby’s head and body are in a straight line, and they are held close, facing your breast.
Bring your baby to the breast and let them latch. With their nose level with your nipple and chin touching your breast, their mouth should be wide open. You should see more dark skin above their top lip than below their bottom lip.
It is not safe to breastfeed in a sling or carrier. Take your baby out first.

## Is my baby getting enough
Signs of enough milk: rapid sucks then longer ones, rounded cheeks, swallowing you can hear, a settled baby who comes off the breast alone, and a content baby after most feeds.
After the first few days your baby should have at least 6 wet nappies a day. After about 3 days the poo changes from black and thick to soft or runny and yellow or mustard.
It is normal for babies to lose a little weight in the first week. Talk to your midwife or health visitor if you are worried about weight gain.

## Help
Midwives, health visitors and trained local peer supporters can help. You can call the National Breastfeeding Helpline on 0300 100 0212, open 24 hours.
Your partner can help by going to sessions, encouraging you, bringing you food and drink, getting involved in baby care, and later giving a bottle of expressed milk.

## When to call your midwife
- You are worried your baby is not getting enough milk
- Your baby falls asleep before deep swallowing, or feeding hurts
- Fewer than 6 wet nappies a day after the first few days
- Your baby is not gaining weight, or is unsettled during or after feeds

## Questions
Q: How often should I feed?
A: As often as your baby wants. At least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours in the first few weeks, and sometimes every hour at first.
Q: Does formula or a dummy affect supply?
A: In the early weeks, before breastfeeding is settled, topping up with formula or giving a dummy can lower your milk supply.
Q: Where can I get help?
A: Your midwife, health visitor or a peer supporter, or the National Breastfeeding Helpline on 0300 100 0212, open 24 hours.

Evidence: Based on WHO and NHS guidance on breastfeeding and the UNICEF Baby Friendly Initiative.
Sources: Benefits of breastfeeding (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/benefits/); Breastfeeding: the first few days (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/the-first-few-days/); Positioning and attachment (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/positioning-and-attachment/); Breastfeeding help and support (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/help-and-support/)

# Safe sleep for newborns
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/newborn-safe-sleep/
Stage: After birth

Safe sleep comes down to a short list. Learn it once and you can rest more easily.

## In short
- On the back: Always put baby to sleep on their back, for every sleep.
- Own space: A firm, flat mattress in a cot or Moses basket in your room for the first six months.
- Keep it clear: No pillows, bumpers, loose blankets or soft toys in the sleep space.
- Avoid risk: Do not sleep with baby on a sofa or armchair, and do not smoke around baby.

## What SIDS is
Sudden infant death syndrome, or SIDS, is the sudden and unexplained death of an apparently healthy baby up to 12 months old. It used to be called cot death.
It is rare, and no one knows what causes it. But some things raise the risk, such as cigarette smoke and sleeping with your baby on a sofa or chair. Babies born before 37 weeks or weighing under 2.5 kg are at higher risk.
It is most likely in the first 6 months and can happen any time a baby is asleep, day or night. If your baby was born early, follow safer sleep advice for a year from the due date, not the birth date.

## Do
Always place your baby on their back to sleep, with their feet at the bottom of the cot or Moses basket. If they roll, move them onto their back until they can roll both ways themselves.
Use a separate cot or Moses basket in the same room as you for every sleep for at least the first 6 months. Use a firm, flat mattress.
Keep the cot clear. No pillows, duvets, bumpers, loose blankets, soft toys, pods or nests.
Breastfeed if you can. Think about a dummy to settle your baby to sleep, as some research suggests it may help lower the risk. Keep your baby’s routine vaccinations up to date.

## Don’t
Do not sleep on a sofa or in an armchair with your baby. Do not smoke when pregnant or around your baby, and do not let anyone smoke in the same room.
Do not let your baby stay in a car seat too long. It is fine to fall asleep while travelling, but take them out as soon as you arrive.

## Not too hot, not too cold
Keep the room between about 16 and 20°C and check with a thermometer. Overheating can raise the risk.
Feel your baby’s chest or the back of their neck. Cool hands and feet are normal. Remove layers if they are hot or sweating. Use lightweight blankets, sheets or a baby sleeping bag.
Never use a hot water bottle or electric blanket, or put your baby next to a radiator, heater or fire or in direct sunlight.

## If you share a bed
The safest place is a separate cot or Moses basket. If you do share a bed, use a firm flat mattress, keep pillows and blankets away, do not swaddle, keep other children and pets out, and make sure your baby cannot fall out or get trapped.
Do not share a bed if your baby was born before 37 weeks or weighed under 2.5 kg. Also do not if you or your partner smoke, have had 2 or more units of alcohol, taken recreational drugs, or taken medicine that makes you drowsy.

## Questions
Q: Is it safe to sleep with my baby on the sofa?
A: No. Sleeping on a sofa or armchair with your baby raises the risk of SIDS.
Q: What temperature should the room be?
A: About 16 to 20°C. Feel your baby’s chest or back of the neck, and remove layers if they feel hot or sweaty.

Evidence: Based on NHS and The Lullaby Trust guidance on safer sleep.
Sources: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/sudden-infant-death-syndrome-sids/)

---

# Postnatal recovery: healing body and mind
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/postnatal-recovery/
Stage: After birth

Your body has done something huge. Give it time to rest and heal, and know which signs need a call.

## In short
- Bleeding: Bleeding for a few weeks is normal. Call if it is very heavy, smells bad or you pass large clots.
- Stitches and soreness: Keep clean and dry, rest, and use pain relief as advised. Call if pain gets worse.
- Pelvic floor: Pelvic floor exercises can help healing. A midwife can show you how.
- Rest and mood: Sleep when you can and accept help. Low mood that lasts more than two weeks needs a talk with your doctor.

## The first weeks
You will bleed from your vagina for a few weeks. It usually stops after 6 to 8 weeks, but can last longer.
Some people feel tummy pain as the womb shrinks, especially when breastfeeding. This is normal.
Midwives visit you at home or in a clinic until your baby is about 10 days old. A health visitor sees you around 10 to 14 days.
Stitches from a tear or episiotomy should heal within about a month. A caesarean takes longer to recover from, and you may need to avoid driving, exercise, heavy lifting and sex for about 6 weeks.

## Moving your body
Gentle exercise helps your body recover and can help you feel more energetic. Walking, gentle stretches, and pelvic floor and tummy exercises are good places to start.
Even a short daily walk with your baby can help you feel less tired.

## Sleep and tiredness
Looking after a baby is tiring, especially in the first months when your baby wakes several times a night. This phase does not last forever. As babies get older they sleep for longer.
Rest when your baby sleeps, even if it means leaving the housework. Share the nights if you can. A partner can do nappies or morning dressing, or give a bottle of expressed milk once breastfeeding is settled.
Ask friends or relatives to watch your baby while you nap. If you are on your own, see if someone can stay a few days.
If you cannot sleep even when your baby sleeps, or feel tired all the time, these can be signs of postnatal depression. Talk to a GP or health visitor.

## Your 6-week check
You should have a postnatal check 6 to 8 weeks after the birth. You can request one yourself, especially if you have worries. Make a list of questions to take.
It usually covers how you are feeling, vaginal discharge and periods, blood pressure if you had problems, an examination if you had stitches or ongoing pain, contraception, and how feeding is going.
Tell your doctor if you feel sad or anxious, have trouble holding in pee or wind, have pain during sex or in the area between your vagina and bottom, or are unsure about your vaccines.

## Contraception
You can have sex as soon as you feel ready. There are no rules. But you can get pregnant from 21 days after birth, even before a period and even if you are breastfeeding.
If you do not want to get pregnant, use contraception from 21 days. If you have had a tear or episiotomy, pain during sex is common in the first few months.

## When to call your midwife
- Sudden, very heavy bleeding, or you feel faint or dizzy. Call 999
- Temperature over 38°C, or bleeding that smells unusual
- Wound or stitches more painful, swollen or leaking pus
- Feeling low, hopeless or very anxious for more than 2 weeks

## Questions
Q: When is my postnatal check?
A: Between 6 and 8 weeks after the birth. You can request one yourself if you have concerns.
Q: How long does bleeding last?
A: Usually 6 to 8 weeks, but it can last longer. Speak to your midwife, GP or health visitor if you are worried.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE postnatal care guidance.
Sources: Early days (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/early-days/); Caesarean section: recovery (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/caesarean-section/recovery/); Episiotomy and perineal tears (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/labour-and-birth/episiotomy-and-perineal-tears/); Sleep and tiredness after having a baby (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/support-and-services/sleep-and-tiredness-after-having-a-baby/); Your 6-week postnatal check (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/support-and-services/your-6-week-postnatal-check/)

# Baby blues or postnatal depression: signs and help
URL: https://miapregnancy.com/learn/postnatal-depression/
Stage: After birth

Many new parents feel low. This guide covers the difference between baby blues and depression, and how to get help fast.

## In short
- Baby blues: Tearfulness and mood swings in the first two weeks are common and pass.
- Postnatal depression: If low mood, anxiety or feeling unable to cope lasts more than two weeks, speak to your midwife, health visitor or GP.
- Partners too: Partners can also feel low. Help is for them as well.
- Urgent help: If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, call your GP, 111 or 999 now.

## What it is
Postnatal depression is a common mental health condition that can happen after having a baby. It usually gets better with treatment.
It can begin while you are pregnant, soon after birth, or up to a year after. Fathers and partners can have it too.

## The signs
Low mood, finding it hard to enjoy anything, feeling hopeless or that you cannot cope, and feeling guilty, worthless or like a bad parent.
Feeling fearful, anxious or worrying all the time, restless or irritable, with trouble sleeping even when you have time to rest.
Difficulty concentrating, difficult feelings about your baby or trouble bonding, and thoughts of suicide or harming yourself or your baby.

## Baby blues or something more
Feeling down, anxious or irritable for a few days after birth is very common. It is called the baby blues and usually goes within 2 weeks.
If it continues, gets worse or you are struggling to cope, get help. It is important to get help even if you only have some of the signs.

## Getting help
Speak to your GP, midwife or health visitor. You can also refer yourself to NHS talking therapies if you are 18 or over, with no GP referral needed.
Tell your doctor at your 6-week check if you feel sad or anxious. You do not need to struggle alone or put on a brave face, and it does not mean you are a bad parent.
You may fear your baby will be taken away if you ask for help. This is very rare. Your care team will support you to care for your baby.

## Treatment
Treatment includes talking therapies such as CBT and antidepressants. Many antidepressants are safe while breastfeeding. Tell your doctor you are breastfeeding and they will choose a suitable one.
It usually gets better in 3 to 6 months, though it can last longer. It is more likely to get better with treatment.

## What you can do
Talk about how you feel with a friend, family member, health professional or counsellor. You can call Samaritans on 116 123. Ask for help with shopping, chores and childcare.
Get regular exercise, even a short walk, and go to a local support group or parent and baby group. Rest and sleep as much as you can, and make time for things you enjoy.
Do not use illegal drugs or alcohol to manage your symptoms.

## When to call your midwife
- You feel low, hopeless or very anxious for more than 2 weeks. See your GP, midwife or health visitor
- You have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Get urgent help now. Call 999 or Samaritans on 116 123
- You cannot sleep even when your baby sleeps

## Questions
Q: Is it the baby blues or postnatal depression?
A: The baby blues usually go within 2 weeks of the birth. If low feelings continue, get worse, or you are struggling to cope, talk to your GP, midwife or health visitor.
Q: Will my baby be taken away if I ask for help?
A: This is very rare. Your care team will give you the support you need to care for your baby.
Q: Can partners get it?
A: Yes. Fathers and partners can also have depression after having a baby.

Evidence: Based on NHS and NICE guidance on perinatal mental health.
Sources: Postnatal depression (https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/postnatal-depression/); Your 6-week postnatal check (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/support-and-services/your-6-week-postnatal-check/)
